articles.title: Lateral Opening-Wedge Versus Medial Closing-Wedge Distal Femoral Osteotomy for Adolescent Idiopathic Genu Valgum: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Khatri JP, Ghosh AK, Parmar RS, Gopinathan NR, Sudesh P, Rangasamy K, et al.
articles.population: Adolescents aged 12 to 18 years with idiopathic genu valgum (knock knees) after distal femoral physeal closure
articles.outcomes: Mechanical axis deviation at radiographic union, pain, functional scores (Pedi-IKDC), satisfaction, union time, hospital stay, return to activity, and complications
articles.take_home: Medial closing-wedge osteotomy achieved slightly better alignment correction than lateral opening-wedge osteotomy, but this difference was not clinically meaningful. Both techniques successfully corrected the deformity with similar pain relief, satisfaction, and recovery outcomes.

articles.title: Beyond surgery: a scoping review of pharmaceutical approaches in treating congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia.
articles.authors: Madegowda A, Barik S, Garg V, Agarwal A
articles.population: Children with congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia
articles.sample_size: 13 studies included; individual study sample sizes ranged from 2 to 39 participants
articles.outcomes: Bone union rates, refracture rates, and complications
articles.take_home: Bone morphogenetic protein 2 combined with bisphosphonates shows promise for achieving bone union in congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia, with near-complete union rates within 3 to 9 months and fewer refractures. However, the evidence comes from small specialised studies, so these results should be interpreted cautiously.

articles.title: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium in adolescent athletes with acute groin pain: clinical and MRI features of a radiograph-occult injury pattern.
articles.authors: Sakoda S, Kajiwara K, Nagaoka R, Kawano K
articles.population: Young athletes aged 22 years or under with acute sports-related groin pain
articles.outcomes: Return to unrestricted sports participation; mean time to return 4.5 weeks; associated injuries with anterior inferior iliac spine avulsion or iliacus injury in 50%
articles.take_home: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is an injury to the hip bone that shows up on MRI scans but not on standard X-rays in young athletes with groin pain. All patients recovered with non-operative treatment and returned to sport within an average of 4.5 weeks.

articles.title: Preoperative ultrasound in pediatric supracondylar fracture-related nerve injuries: intraoperative correlation in a tertiary referral retrospective case series.
articles.authors: Abukar A, Alfonso Palanca P, Yogarajah N, Sugand K, Pressney I, Panagiotidou A, et al.
articles.population: Children under 16 years with persistent nerve palsy after supracondylar humeral fracture
articles.outcomes: Ultrasound detection of nerve abnormality and agreement with intraoperative findings
articles.take_home: Ultrasound detected nerve problems in 95% of children with persistent nerve palsy after fracture, but did not accurately identify the specific type of nerve injury compared to what surgeons found during surgery. Ultrasound should be used alongside clinical assessment rather than as the sole guide for deciding whether surgery is needed.

articles.title: Trisomy 21 and Patellar Femoral Instability in a Pediatric Population: Results From 53,800 Patients.
articles.authors: Magoline JA, Yoder RG, Morscher MA, Riley PM Jr, Bono KT, Polousky JD, et al.
articles.study_type: Retrospective cohort analysis using electronic health records
articles.population: Children with Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) aged 19 or under, compared with matched children without Trisomy 21
articles.sample_size: 53,800 patients with Trisomy 21; 347 with patellofemoral instability matched with 347 without Trisomy 21
articles.outcomes: Annual prevalence of patellofemoral instability and rates of surgical intervention between groups
articles.take_home: Children with Down syndrome and knee instability (patellofemoral instability) are nearly twice as likely to need surgery compared to other children with the same knee problem, although the overall rate of the condition is lower than previously thought. Girls with Down syndrome are more affected than boys.

articles.title: Osteochondral lesions of the talus in the pediatric population: A practical narrative review.
articles.authors: Turati M, Gatti SD, Thusing M, Guelfi M, Crippa M, Sinikumpu J, et al.
articles.population: Children and adolescents with osteochondral lesions of the talus
articles.outcomes: Assessment and treatment approaches for osteochondral lesions of the talus; comparison of imaging modalities; surgical and non-operative management outcomes
articles.take_home: Osteochondral lesions of the talus cause persistent ankle pain in children after injury and may occur without clear trauma. MRI is needed to properly detect and assess these lesions, and treatment depends on whether the fragment is stable, with non-operative management tried first but showing variable results, whilst surgery options include drilling, bone marrow stimulation, or fragment fixation depending on the lesion characteristics.
